food.text: Aboriginal Australians ate native animal and plant foods for an estimated 60,000 years of human habitation on the continent. An estimated 4,999 species of native food were used by Aboriginal peoples. This food tradition is now called bush tucker.

The typical Aboriginal diet included kangaroo, emu, wombats, goanna, snakes and birds. It also included many insects such as honey ants, bogong moths and witchetty grubs. Plant foods included taro, coconuts, nuts, fruits and berries.

Aboriginal Australians were complex hunter-gatherers with diverse economies. Certain groups engaged in fire-stick farming and fish farming, and built semi-permanent shelters. How far some groups practised agriculture is still controversial.

The ancestors of today's Torres Strait Islanders arrived from Papua New Guinea and settled the islands about 2,500 years ago. A distinctive maritime culture emerged, and agriculture also developed on some of the islands.

Native Australian plant foods include fruits such as quandong and kutjera, and spices such as lemon myrtle. Others are the leafy vegetable warrigal greens and various native yams. The macadamia nut is the best-known bush tucker plant.

Much native food was unsafe or unpalatable raw, so Aboriginal peoples processed it. They cooked on open fires, boiled food in bark containers, pounded vegetables and seeds, and hung bags in running water. Toxic seeds, such as Cycas media and Moreton Bay chestnut, were processed to remove the toxins and make them safe to eat. Some animals, such as kangaroos, were cooked in their own skins, and others, such as turtles, in their own shells.

Each day the women of the group went into successive parts of one countryside carrying wooden digging sticks and plaited dilly bags or wooden coolamons. Larger animals and birds such as kangaroos and emus were speared or disabled with a thrown club, boomerang or stone. The non-returnable boomerang, known more correctly as a Throwing Stick, was more powerful than the returning kind and could injure or even kill a kangaroo.
On the Australian mainland no animal other than the dingo was domesticated. Torres Strait Islanders, however, also used domestic pigs and cassowaries.
Aboriginal men were excellent trackers and stalkers. They stayed downwind of their prey and would freeze and crawl when in the open. Some even covered themselves with mud to disguise their smell.

art.text: Aboriginal art is believed to be the oldest continuing tradition of art in the world. Evidence of Indigenous Australian art can be traced back at least 30,000 years, so the art made in the Classical era belongs to an unbroken line reaching far into the past.

Australia has three major regional styles of ancient rock art. There is a geometric style of concentric circles, arcs and dots in Central Australia, Tasmania, the Kimberley and Victoria, a simple figurative style in Queensland, and a complex figurative style in Arnhem Land that includes X-ray art.

In Arnhem Land X-ray painting, the female form, especially the womb, appears prominently at some famous sites. The mimi, spirits said to have taught the art of painting to Aboriginal people, and ancestors are "released" through these artworks.

The Sydney rock engravings, found in places such as Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, are approximately 5000 to 200 years old. Some of them were therefore carved during the Classical era, in what is now a major city.

Australian cave art is comparable in age and abundance to that of Lascaux and Altamira in Europe. Designs across the continent generally carry significance linked to the spirituality of the Dreamtime.

The ancestors of today's Torres Strait Islanders arrived from what is now Papua New Guinea around 2,500 years ago, settling islands at the northern tip of Australia. Torres Strait Islanders are known for their traditional sculpture and headgear, which the National Gallery of Australia exhibits.

science.text: Australian Aboriginal astronomy has been passed down orally, through ceremonies, and in artwork of many kinds. It shows a deep understanding of how celestial objects move, and people used it to make calendars and to navigate across the continent and its waters. Aboriginal peoples have been described as the "world's first astronomers".

Some Aboriginal constellations are named for dark patches in the sky rather than for the points of light made by stars. The Emu in the Sky is one example. Other constellations are named for their shapes, such as the Pleiades, Orion and the Milky Way.

Many groups in northern Australia use a calendar with six seasons, and some mark the seasons by the stars visible during them. For the Pitjantjatjara, the rising of the Pleiades at dawn in May marks the start of winter. Aboriginal calendars therefore tend to differ from European ones.

Stars also told Aboriginal Australians when to move on or look for new food. The Boorong people in Victoria know that when the Malleefowl (Lyra) disappears in October, to "sit with the Sun", it is time to start gathering her eggs on Earth.

Star calendars were linked to animals and trade. Some groups know that when Orion first appears in the sky, dingo puppies are about to be born. When Scorpius appears, the Yolŋu know that Macassan fishermen will soon arrive to fish for trepang.

The Torres Strait channel is 150 km wide, yet it stayed readily navigable. The chain of Torres Strait Islands and reefs gave seafarers stopping points along the way. Islanders settled over 2500 years ago, and cultural interaction continued with the Aboriginal people of northeast Australia.

philosophy.text: Australian Aboriginal spirituality includes the Dreaming, songlines and oral literature, all performed in ceremonies by each language group across Australia. These stories describe each group's local cultural landscape and give meaning to the topography of the whole country.

Custodianship rests on a strong traditional connection to lands and seas known collectively as Country. A custodian has a responsibility to care for Country, which reflects a worldview not necessarily compatible with Western ideas of land ownership and the right to property.
The Emu in the Sky is a constellation used almost everywhere in Aboriginal culture, made of dark nebulae against the Milky Way. Its head is the Coalsack Nebula, next to the Southern Cross.

Among the Murrinh-Patha people, no distinction is drawn between the spiritual and the material, or between the sacred and the profane. All life is sacred, all conduct has moral implication, and all meaning arises from the ever-present Dreaming.

Mary Graham, a Kombu-merra and Wakka Wakka woman, developed the idea of an Aboriginal custodial ethic. She holds that Aboriginal Australians saw land as the only constant in human lives, so the physical and spiritual worlds were regarded as interconnected. People were obliged to look after the land and renew its flora and fauna.

Traditional Aboriginal religions were animist and tended to include elements of ancestor worship. The Rainbow Serpent is a major dream spirit for Aboriginal people across Australia, while the Yowie and Bunyip are other well known dream spirits.

Stanner characterised the philosophy behind Murrinh-Patha myths as a belief that life is a joyous thing with maggots at its centre. Life is good and benevolent, yet each person must come to understand and endure painful suffering while growing. This gives Murrinh-Patha people motive and meaning in life.

Mircea Eliade wrote that indigenous Australians generally believe the world, people, animals and plants were created by Supernatural beings. Afterwards these beings disappeared, either ascending to the sky or entering the earth. Aboriginal beliefs are linked to the land and to certain sites of significance.

Aboriginal religion has ritual systems that emphasise life transitions such as adulthood and death. Beliefs and spirituality are intrinsically linked to the land generally and to certain sites of significance in particular.

Torres Strait Islander religion bore similarities to broader Melanesian spirituality. This sets it apart from the Aboriginal beliefs of the Dreaming, reflecting the distinct heritage of these Indigenous Australians.

culture.text: The ancestors of today's Torres Strait Islanders arrived from what is now Papua New Guinea around 2,500 years ago. They settled the islands on the northern tip of the Australian landmass, giving the region a distinct culture from Aboriginal Australians.

Ceremonies have been part of Aboriginal culture since the beginning. They include Dreaming stories, secret events at sacred sites, homecomings, births and deaths, and most involve dance, song, ritual and elaborate body decoration or costume.

Aboriginal art has existed for thousands of years, ranging from ancient rock art to modern watercolour landscapes. Ancient Aboriginal rock art shows ceremonies and traditions that are still continued today.

The Torres Strait Islander people permanently settled their islands at least 2,500 years ago. They were seafarers who lived off seasonal horticulture and the resources of their reefs and seas. They were culturally and linguistically distinct from mainland Aboriginal peoples.

In Arnhem Land and Central Australia, ceremonies are performed to ensure a plentiful supply of foods. In many regions they also educate children, passing on the lore, spiritual beliefs and survival skills of their people, and some mark adolescents' rite of passage.

The ancestors of today's Torres Strait Islanders arrived from Papua New Guinea about 2,500 years ago, and a distinctive Torres Strait Islander maritime culture emerged. Agriculture also developed on some of the islands.

Aboriginal peoples did not develop a system of writing before colonisation. Instead, lore, the customs and stories passed down through the generations, was learned from childhood and set the rules for how to interact with the land, kinship and community.
